optimistic

/op-tih-MIS-tik/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Optimistic means hopeful and confident about future outcomes.

After the early rains, the farmers were optimistic about the best harvest in a decade.

Example

The team had lost its two best players to graduation, and the local paper predicted a last-place finish. Coach Ferreira disagreed — cheerfully, specifically, and out loud. "We return our whole defense, our schedule favors us in October, and our freshmen are faster than anyone knows," she told the booster club. "I'm optimistic, and I'll tell you exactly why." She expected good things, and she had reasons.

Ferreira's confident expectation of a good season — backed by reasons and aimed at the future — is precisely the hopeful confidence that optimistic describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hopeful: Hopeful means wanting a good outcome and holding on to the chance of it, even when the odds look poor. Optimistic goes a step further: it actually expects things to go well, with confidence behind the hope. Hope keeps the door open; optimism walks through it expecting good news.

confident: Confident means feeling sure — of success or of your own abilities — and it can apply to anything, including the present moment. Optimistic points at the future: it blends confidence with hope, expecting things to turn out well. You are confident in a skill; you are optimistic about tomorrow.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

pessimistic: expecting the worst

defeatist: accepting failure in advance

Where it sits · how confidently a good outcome is expected

wishful → optimistic → starry-eyed

wishful vs. optimistic: Wishful means merely wanting a good outcome, with no real expectation behind the want; optimistic means actually expecting one, with confidence behind the hope.

starry-eyed vs. optimistic: Starry-eyed overshoots optimistic — the confidence has come detached from evidence, hope with the brakes removed.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — optim: best (Latin optimus)

Suffix — -istic: relating to a belief or practice of

Put it together: Optimistic grows from Latin optimus, 'best' — the root of optimum and optimal. Eighteenth-century philosophers coined 'optimism' for the belief that we live in the best of all possible worlds; the everyday word kept the kernel: an optimistic person expects the best version of the future to be the one that actually shows up.

Use the root in a new word: optimum: Engineers spent the final week tuning the engine toward its optimum before race day.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral, everyday; the standard word for forward-looking hope

Optimistic sits between plain hope and blind faith: it expects a good outcome with some confidence, and unlike this unit's joy words (ecstatic, euphoric) it describes an outlook on the future rather than happiness felt right now.
